1:
Augustine of Hippo makes the order of the two words the point: God neither loses the severity of judgment in the bounty of mercy nor loses the bounty of mercy in judging severely, and the psalmist says mercy and judgment rather than the reverse because mercy goes before. John Calvin names that interpretation and sets it aside: David is not praising God for punishing and sparing but declaring in solemn terms what kind of king he means to be when the promised sovereignty comes to him. Charles Ellicott agrees that the two are the especially requisite attributes of a good monarch, though first regarded ideally as attributes of the divine King, and quotes the line that earthly power shows likest God’s when mercy seasons justice. Adam Clarke offers both readings, that adverse and prosperous providences have alike been useful to his soul, or that on coming to the government of all the tribes he resolves on benevolence to the upright and judgment on the wicked. C.H. Spurgeon insists on the harder half, that we ought as much to bless the Lord for the judgment with which he chastens sin as for the mercy with which he forgives it, since there is as much love in the blows of his hand as in the kisses of his mouth. Matthew Henry takes the psalm for a pattern of a good magistrate and a good master of a family together.

The half-line asking when God will come is the crux, and the two closest readers stand opposed. Keil and Delitzsch place the psalm in the period when the ark stood in the house where David had left it after the misfortune that frightened him, and hear behind the clause his own words then, that he did not venture to bring the ark within range of his house. Charles Ellicott calls that reminiscence far-fetched, and reports that the clause is so awkward, however translated, that some critics pronounce it spurious; in the older writings the coming of God to a person is associated with punishment or inquisition. He would take the verb as third person, with the perfect way as its subject, and the interrogative as a simple adverb of time, giving the sense that he will give heed to a guileless way whenever it comes to him — that is, whenever a course of action presents an alternative, he will choose the better. Adam Clarke keeps the received sense and turns it into dependence: he can neither walk in the perfect way nor grow wise unto salvation unless God comes to him by grace and Spirit. John Wesley notes that God is often said to come to men when he fulfils a promise to them.

On behaving wisely Charles Ellicott gives the literal sense as looking to a guileless way, and notes that the root is that of a familiar psalm-title, so that some find a reference to music here; but he thinks the received rendering right, since words like provident and circumspect show how the idea of caution and then of wisdom grows out of looking. John Gill observes that David did behave so before he came to the throne, which made Saul fear him and the people love him, but that no man lives without sin, so the words are most applicable to Christ, of whom it was prophesied that he should deal prudently. Adam Clarke presses the walk within the house hardest, translating it as setting oneself to walk, a determined point: it is easier for most men to walk with a perfect heart in the church, or even in the world, than in their own families, and how many are as meek as lambs among others who at home are wasps or tigers. Charles Ellicott makes the same application generally, that piety should begin at home and religion show itself in the household as much as at church.
3:
Adam Clarke reads the resolutions as a programme of government and spells them out: no unjust wars, no sinful alliances, no oppression of subjects by excessive taxation to support extravagance in the court, and no place of political trust for those who apostatize from the true religion or live without its influence. Charles Ellicott marks the wisdom of such a resolve in a despotic monarch, who has only to speak in order to effect whatever he has looked on with desire, and renders the object of the vow a thing, or word, of worthlessness. John Gill takes the eyes both ways, of the body, which are the inlets of lust and easily caught by objects that inflame the heart, and of the mind.

On the froward heart John Gill describes the man rather than the disposition: one who devises perversity and speaks it out, contrary to the light of nature and the word of God and to the sentiments of all good men, and so a disagreeable companion. Adam Clarke narrows it to a question of appointments, that rash and headstrong men shall not be employed and that no countenance shall be given to sinners of any kind. John Wesley puts it in six words, that such shall be turned out of the court and neither owned nor countenanced.

The private slanderer draws the entry’s longest note. Adam Clarke reports a striking rendering from the Chaldee, that the man speaks with a triple tongue against his neighbour — a tongue by which he slays three persons, the man he slanders, the man to whom he tells it, and himself — so that every slander inflicts three deadly wounds; and he adds that Jerome said nearly the same, that the detractor ruins both himself and the one who listens to him. He treats the class as enemies of the state, flatterers and time-servers who undermine the upright in order to get their offices, and would expel them from his court, with the haughty after them, since the Hebrew says simply, I cannot. Charles Ellicott notes the same idiom and that the proud heart is literally a broad one, extended with pride, though the Greek and Latin make it insatiable; he observes that the informer and the haughty favourite are no unknown characters in an eastern court. John Gill takes the cutting off as exclusion from all communion and conversation, and then notices that David did not keep his own rule, since he listened to the slanders of Ziba against Mephibosheth; only Christ, who knows the hearts and the secret actions of men, will reject every person of that character.
6:
Adam Clarke continues to read the psalm as a personnel policy. The eyes on the faithful mean approbation, and those approved are to be his confidants and privy counsellors; no irreligious or wicked man, whatever his abilities, shall be countenanced or supported, and the court is to be purified of the base, the avaricious, the venal and the profligate, while the man who walks in a perfect way shall be prime minister and chief officer over the army and the finances. Charles Ellicott gives the idiom exactly: to tarry in his sight is to stand as a courtier in the royal presence, and against the deceitful courtier he sets the Greek poet’s line that the man who hides one thing in his mind and speaks another is hateful as the gates of hell. John Gill turns the whole to Christ, whose eyes are on faithful ministers and faithful members alike, to keep them and to reward them.

On the worker of deceit Adam Clarke promises to expel every sycophant and flatterer, and puts two emperors side by side to show what is at stake: one encouraged flatterers, while the other burned some, banished others and sold many for slaves. John Gill extends the class from courtiers to hypocrites who have only a form of godliness and to false teachers, none of whom shall have place in Christ’s house below or above. The last verse turns on a single word. Charles Ellicott renders it literally in the morning, and reports the suggestion that it refers to the eastern custom of holding courts of law early in the day; he adds that the city must bear out its name in its character. John Gill takes the Hebrew the same way but draws a different sense, that the destroying is to be done every morning, constantly and continually, and that a general reformation of the kingdom is intended. John Wesley reads it simply as speedily, as soon as he is seated on the throne, and Adam Clarke as taking the first opportunity — adding that an administration must have been a good one where such pious caution was used in choosing all the officers of the state.
